title: verdict
description: The grader's output, produced under constrained decoding. FIELD ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: the model emits fields in schema order, so the order here is the order it is forced to think in. `claims` comes first so technical content is extracted BEFORE any score exists to rationalise towards - the correctness penalty measured against non-native phrasing is the reason. Within a dimension the same principle applies: evidence, then reasoning, then score. TWO FIELDS ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT. `recommendation` is a pure function of `overall`, and asking the model for it produced strong_yes on candidates scored 2 of 5 in two runs. `overall` was here and emitted BEFORE `dimensions`, which meant the model committed to a headline number before producing a single dimension score - the exact inversion of evidence-then-score - and then rationalised underneath it. On a real interview it returned overall 3 while scoring the four dimensions 4, 4, 4, 3, and a human reviewer independently gave the same four dimension scores and an overall of 4. Both fields are now computed from what the model actually produced. Constrained decoding guarantees shape, not coherence between fields.

claims.description: Every checkable technical assertion the candidate made, extracted before anything is scored. Restate each one plainly in your own words - stripping the phrasing is the point, because a claim is true or false independently of how fluently it was said.

claim.description: The assertion, restated plainly. Not a quote: a quote carries the phrasing back in, which is what this field exists to remove.

status.description: Judge the technical content only. `unverifiable` is for claims about the candidate's own history, which cannot be checked and must not be counted as either right or wrong.

evidence.description: Quote or closely paraphrase what the candidate actually said. Write this before deciding a score.

reasoning.description: How that evidence maps to the rubric.

score.description: Integer from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). Must follow from the evidence above. For correctness, score the claims list: how many are `correct` against how many are `incorrect`. Phrasing, grammar and fluency are not evidence about correctness and must not move this number.
